prompt: What does Binary Authorization check when Cloud Run is asked to run an image?
hint: It decides nothing about safety itself.

choices.text: That the image has no critical vulnerability
choices.why: It reads no scan; a signature may stand for one, but the check is the signature.

choices.text: Signatures by the required attestors over that exact digest
choices.why: Right. Signatures over one digest, and nothing else.

choices.text: That the image's labels name an approved team
choices.why: Labels are not read; anybody can write a label.

choices.text: That the tag matches a release in Cloud Deploy
choices.why: Binary Authorization knows nothing of Cloud Deploy's releases.

prompt: A team wants to know which running images their new policy would refuse, before refusing any. Which setting?

choices.text: evaluationMode: ALWAYS_ALLOW
choices.why: That allows everything and evaluates nothing, so it reports nothing.

choices.text: enforcementMode: DRYRUN_AUDIT_LOG_ONLY
choices.why: Right. It writes what would have been refused and refuses nothing.

choices.text: globalPolicyEvaluationMode: ENABLE
choices.why: That exempts Google's system images; it has nothing to do with dry run.

choices.text: evaluationMode: ALWAYS_DENY for a week
choices.why: That refuses every deployment, the opposite of a rehearsal.

prompt: The shop's policy requires attestations. A developer deploys a new Cloud Run service without `--binary-authorization`, with an unsigned image. What happens, and what closes the gap?

choices.text: Refused: a project policy applies to every service
choices.why: Cloud Run consults it only on services where it is turned on.

choices.text: Refused, unless the developer uses break-glass
choices.why: There is nothing to break: the service never asked the policy.

choices.text: It runs; an org-wide constraint closes the gap
choices.why: Right. The constraint makes the flag compulsory for every service.

choices.text: It runs, and continuous validation stops it within the hour
choices.why: Continuous validation is GKE's, and it reports rather than stops.

prompt: At 3 a.m. an unsigned hotfix is deployed with break-glass. What makes that acceptable?

choices.text: Break-glass images are scanned before they run
choices.why: Break-glass skips the policy; nothing extra is checked.

choices.text: Break-glass works only for an owner of the project
choices.why: Whoever can deploy can annotate a deployment; what matters is the record.

choices.text: The audit log records it, and somebody reviews it in the morning
choices.why: Right. The door exists, and opening it leaves a record.

choices.text: Break-glass deployments expire after one hour
choices.why: They do not expire; the image runs until somebody replaces it.

hint: Look at what the command named.

choices.text: The tag a1b2c3d
choices.why: The command named a digest; the tag is only how a person found it.

choices.text: The source code in api/
choices.why: cosign never saw the source; it signs an image in a registry.

choices.text: One image digest
choices.why: Right. And the payload printed by verify names it.

choices.text: Every image in the repository shop/api
choices.why: A signature covers one digest, no more.

prompt: After the signed image was replaced under the same tag, `cosign verify` on the tag said "no signatures found". Why?
hint: What did cosign resolve the tag to?

choices.text: Its new digest was never signed
choices.why: Right. The old signature is still there, over the old digest.

choices.text: Pushing again deleted the signature
choices.why: The .sig artifact is untouched; it is about another digest.

choices.text: The key pair expired when the image changed
choices.why: Keys do not expire with images.

choices.text: Verification by tag is not supported
choices.why: It is supported: cosign resolves the tag and checks that digest.

prompt: In this lab the private key is a file with an empty password. Where does a real signing key belong, and why?

choices.text: In the repository, so the build can read it
choices.why: Then everybody who can read the repository can sign anything.

choices.text: On the laptop of the person who approves releases
choices.why: A laptop is copied, lost and shared; and the signature would no longer stand for the build.

choices.text: In an environment variable of the build
choices.why: It would appear in the build's configuration and in anything that prints its environment.

choices.text: In Cloud KMS, used by name
choices.why: Right. The private half never leaves Google, and only granted accounts can sign.

prompt: cosign stores a signature in the registry beside the image, under a tag made of the digest and the suffix `.___`.
hint: Three letters, in the tags list.

prompt: Why does the shop have two attestors rather than one key the build uses for everything?
hint: A signature is worth the decision behind it.

choices.text: Binary Authorization requires at least two
choices.why: One attestor is allowed; the reason is what each one means.

choices.text: Each signature stands for one decision
choices.why: Right. A build that signed everything would sign a vulnerable image too.

choices.text: Two keys make each signature twice as hard to forge
choices.why: Each signature is as strong as its own key; the point is what they assert.

choices.text: One is for GKE and one for Cloud Run
choices.why: Both platforms read the same policy and both attestors.

prompt: `scan_gate.py` exits with 1 for an image with a fixable critical finding. What stops that image reaching production?
hint: Follow the exit status, then the policy.

choices.text: Artifact Registry refuses to serve it
choices.why: The registry serves it as before; findings block nothing.

choices.text: scan_gate.py deletes the image
choices.why: It only exits; nothing in it touches the registry.

choices.text: No scan-passed attestation is ever made
choices.why: Right. The exit stops the signing, and the missing signature stops the deployment.

choices.text: Cloud Deploy notices the failed build and skips the release
choices.why: Cloud Deploy reads no build results; the refusal is Binary Authorization's.

prompt: An engineer is granted `roles/cloudkms.signerVerifier` on the `scan-passed` key "to help debug". What does that change?
hint: The policy checks a signature, not the hand that made it.

choices.text: Nothing: only the build's account appears in the policy
choices.why: The policy names an attestor, i.e. a key; it names no account.

choices.text: They can read the private key and copy it
choices.why: KMS never releases the private half; but signing with it is enough.

choices.text: They can approve Cloud Deploy rollouts
choices.why: That needs clouddeploy.approver, a different role.

choices.text: They can attest any image as scanned
choices.why: Right. Only the key's audit log would show who signed.

prompt: An image admitted on Monday gets a critical finding on Thursday. What does GKE's continuous validation do?

choices.text: Writes a log entry saying the pod would be refused now
choices.why: Right. Stopping a service is left to a person, from the report.

choices.text: Evicts the pod at once
choices.why: It reports and does not stop anything.

choices.text: Re-signs the image if the scan passes again
choices.why: It signs nothing; signing is the build's.

choices.text: Nothing: admission is checked only once
choices.why: That is what happens without continuous validation, which is why it exists.

prompt: Put the life of the shop's image in order, from build to admission.
hint: A signature comes after the decision it stands for.
items: The tests pass and the image is pushed
The scan finishes on the digest
The scan gate signs as scan-passed
Cloud Run checks both attestations and admits it
trap: Signing scan-passed before the scan finishes is the slip: the signature would assert something nobody had checked.

prompt: Which of these would a policy requiring both attestations refuse? Choose all that apply.
hint: Missing signature, or signature over another digest.

choices.text: An image pushed over a signed tag
choices.why: Yes. Its digest has no attestation.

choices.text: An image built on a laptop and pushed by hand
choices.why: Yes. Nobody with the keys signed it.

choices.text: A signed image deployed with break-glass
choices.why: No. Break-glass admits it, and it was signed anyway.

choices.text: An image the build signed whose scan gate failed
choices.why: Yes. It has one attestation of the two.

choices.text: An image with both attestations and a low finding
choices.why: No. Both signatures are there; the policy reads nothing else.
